notes.trap: A NULL or empty array or map yields zero rows, so the whole input row silently disappears; use `explode_outer(...)` to keep it. When used on a map it produces two columns named `key` and `value`, not one.
notes.example_sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT explode(CAST(NULL AS ARRAY<INT>)) AS x)

notes.trap: Unlike `explode(...)`, a NULL or empty collection produces exactly one row whose generated column is NULL. Downstream counts therefore see an extra row, not zero rows.
notes.example_sql: SELECT x FROM (SELECT explode_outer(filter(array(1), v -> v > 5)) AS x)

notes.trap: The generated `pos` column is 0-based, while `element_at(...)` and `array_position(...)` are 1-based. Mixing the two causes off-by-one errors.
For a NULL or empty collection it emits one row in which both `pos` and `col` are NULL. The position is not 0, so filters such as `pos = 0` drop that row.
notes.example_sql: SELECT pos FROM (SELECT posexplode_outer(CAST(NULL AS ARRAY<INT>)))

notes.trap: Output column names come from the struct's field names: a struct built with `named_struct(...)` yields those names, and only `struct(...)` with unnamed values gives col1, col2. A NULL array produces zero rows.
A NULL or empty array of structs yields one row with every struct field set to NULL instead of no rows. This differs from `inline(...)`, which drops the row.
notes.example_sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT inline_outer(CAST(NULL AS ARRAY<STRUCT<a:INT,b:STRING>>)))

notes.trap: Default column names are 0-based (col0, col1, ...), unlike `inline(...)`, which starts at col1. If the value count is not a multiple of n, the last row is padded with NULL. Values that land in the same column must have the same type, because only NULLs are coerced.
notes.example_sql: SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT stack(2, 1, 2, 3)) WHERE col1 IS NULL
